processing: Black, green and white teas plucked from China bushes, with muscatel second flush and a lot style called Moonlight among its named products.
harvest_season: As with other Darjeeling gardens, first flush and second flush are the prized pickings; the second flush is where muscatel character is sought.
appearance_dry: Twisted leaf with some tips; darker and more even in second flush.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber in muscatel second flush, paler in spring lots.
taste_profile: A rose-like fragrance and the muscatel flavour Darjeeling is known for.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Do not oversteep a muscatel lot: the fruit is the point, and tannin hides it.

vintage_note: Sold by year, flush and invoice number, as is usual for Darjeeling, with muscatel second flush lots the most sought after. Drink within a year or two; Moonlight and other named lots vary from one year to the next.
description:
Castleton is a Kurseong garden on the slopes toward Pankhabari, with 170 hectares planted between 980 and 2,300 metres. Among Darjeeling names it is one of the ones people ask for by name, mostly for second flush muscatel.

The tea comes from delicate China bushes, and the range goes beyond black tea to green, white and a lot called Moonlight. That variety means the name alone tells you little: read the label.

The classic cup is a rose-like nose with muscatel fruit. Give it about three minutes in water just off the boil, then taste, because going long only brings out the tannin.

Because of its reputation the name is widely used, so buy lots with a year and invoice number from a seller you trust. Comparing it with Margaret's Hope or Thurbo, which share an owner, is a good lesson in how Darjeeling gardens differ.
history:
The estate was earlier called Kumseri. A building known as Bank Ghar, which looked like a castle, gave the place its later name.

It holds ISO 9000, HACCP and ISO 22000 certifications, and it is one of five Darjeeling estates owned by the Goodricke Group.
